doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Pressure in films, television and commercials
summary: Orchestrating a Warner Brothers film under deadline, and why commercials carry the most pressure and second-guessing.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Is it a high pressure situation, writing for films?

Yeah, it’s an interesting thing, I had to orchestrate an hour’s worth of music for a Warner Brothers film in about two weeks, all while I’m teaching and playing and doing all the other stuff I do. And it was just totally under the gun, and then the release gets delayed by © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

a year. And you wonder what all that was about. I think that the bigger the medium actually the less pressure in some ways. The most pressure is in commercials, in that little thirty second spot. I think advertising agencies, agencies rent offices and hire staff just for that one client and if they lose that client the bottom drops out. Tremendously charged and they try to disperse that pressure to everyone they work with. And then television seems to be next and then movies, once people have made it to that level it seems like they have more of a comfort level with what they’re doing. And for me it actually seemed you were a little less second guessed in movies than you are in television, and a lot less than you are in the commercial world. So it’s interesting. But in all those things you’re dealing with people who probably are sticking their nose a little farther into your thing than what they have any business.
Wow you just anticipated my question. Because you’re usually dealing with non- musicians when you’re doing commercials.
And do you have trouble trying to bring to reality what they’re describing to you?
